headline: Raptors gear sells in bursts, and sticker prices send shoppers across the border.
summary: Toronto is a high-volume, price-aware market, and the whole country is its fanbase. Spend peaks at Black Friday, Boxing Day, Caribana weekend, Diwali and Eid. Canadian prices run well above US ones, which feeds cross-border shopping, resale and knockoffs. Leonard's return should spark a jersey surge, but an injury could cut it short, so lead with team and city graphics that outlast him.

insights.title: Canada-wide fanbase, GTA-centred retail
insights.detail: As Canada's only NBA team, the Raptors draw demand from Vancouver to Halifax. The 2026 preseason game in Quebec City shows the team courting the whole country. The GTA still concentrates the volume through malls such as Yorkdale, Eaton Centre, Square One in Mississauga and Pacific Mall in Markham.
insights.implication: Toronto pop-ups need a national e-commerce and Fanatics-style wholesale push behind them. Present Raptors product as "Canada's team," not only Toronto's.

insights.title: Ontario HST of 13% and no tax holidays
insights.detail: Ontario charges 13% HST (5% federal plus 8% provincial) on apparel and footwear. There is no recurring tax-free weekend. Children's clothing and footwear is generally zero-rated for the federal portion. Shoppers read ticket prices as pre-tax and notice every CAD jump.
insights.implication: Clean CAD price points sell: $99, $149 and $229. Use promotion calendars for volume, not tax gimmicks, and keep a visible kids' range.

insights.title: Sale culture is Black Friday and Boxing Day
insights.detail: Boxing Day (Dec 26) is a Canadian retail institution, and Black Friday has become a Canadian peak too. Retailers such as Sport Chek and the Eaton Centre stores run deep markdowns. Many fans wait for these sales, which trains them to expect discounts on team gear.
insights.implication: Sell hero Raptors and Kawhi drops at full price until late November. Make a separate sale tier or outlet-friendly line for Boxing Day, so core product keeps its value.

insights.title: Caribana weekend drives summer spend
insights.detail: Caribana, the Toronto Caribbean Carnival, falls around the first weekend of August and the Civic Holiday. It is a major fashion and costume spending moment for the Caribbean community. Toronto's South Asian, East African and Filipino communities have their own heritage and wedding seasons. The offseason isn't dead for Raptors-adjacent apparel.
insights.implication: Use summer for Toronto-first lifestyle collections (colour, mesh, lightweight pieces) and community collaborations, not only team-licensed product.

insights.title: Winter dictates the product mix
insights.detail: Toronto's cold, wet winter runs roughly November to March, with sleet and slush. Outerwear, hoodies, toques and waterproof footwear sell in season, while shorts and tees peak May to September. Fans commute by TTC and walk the PATH and downtown to games.
insights.implication: Build the City Edition and fan range around layers: warm-up jackets, fleece, beanies and water-resistant shells. Add a late-spring Playoffs shorts-and-tee capsule.

insights.title: Cross-border and resale arbitrage
insights.detail: Canadian prices, exchange rates and duty push shoppers to buy sneakers and jerseys in the US, at Buffalo-area outlets or online. Others go to resale: StockX, GOAT, Kijiji, Facebook Marketplace, Instagram. Toronto has a deep reselling and sneaker-shop scene, and resellers and fans alike buy the drops.
insights.implication: The answer is Canadian-exclusive colourways and Nike app SNKRS access at fair CAD prices. Consider Canada-only Raptors items that crossing the border can't match.

insights.title: Jersey buying follows player moments
insights.detail: Jersey sales spike around signature moments: Kawhi's 2019 run, Vince Carter's return and now Leonard's homecoming after a 46-win season, with Scottie Barnes as the franchise face. Kids' and youth sizes, cheaper replica-style tees and unlicensed market knockoffs compete with authentic and swingman jerseys.
insights.implication: Stock kids' and swingman first and keep a limited authentic tier. Pair player jerseys with evergreen "Toronto" and "We The North" pieces.

places.name: CF Toronto Eaton Centre
places.why: The default downtown stop for sneakers, apparel and tourist traffic, with a heavy Boxing Day crowd.

places.name: Yorkdale Shopping Centre
places.why: The high-end, sneaker-heavy mall for affluent, style-led shoppers, and a core Nike and drop-day location.

places.name: Square One Shopping Centre
places.why: The suburban hub for the large Peel Region market, home to many South Asian and Caribbean families.

places.name: Scotiabank Arena
places.why: Home of the Raptors and the gameday merchandise point of sale. Maple Leaf Square outside draws the watch-party crowds.

places.name: Kensington Market and Queen West
places.why: Vintage, streetwear and independent shops that set local style and serve resale-minded buyers.

places.name: Pacific Mall
places.why: A hub for the Chinese Canadian community, with many independent vendors. Unlicensed apparel is a retail risk to watch across value markets.

people.name: Kawhi Leonard
people.role: Raptors forward, 2019 champion and Finals MVP
people.why: His return is Toronto's biggest merchandise story of the year, and it revives 2019 nostalgia.

people.name: Scottie Barnes
people.why: The franchise face and the long-term jersey bet for kids and younger fans.

people.name: Drake
people.role: Rapper, OVO founder and Raptors global ambassador
people.why: OVO's apparel made Raptors-adjacent fashion a global style signal, and any Nike collaboration talk runs through his orbit.

people.name: Masai Ujiri
people.role: Giants of Africa founder; former Raptors president (left June 2025)
people.why: A trusted civic and community figure whose Giants of Africa work carries weight with Black and African Canadians, even after MLSE parted ways with him in June 2025.

people.name: Roots Canada
people.why: A homegrown rival in heritage and team-adjacent apparel that shapes expectations for Canadian-made quality.

moments.name: Raptors home opener (date to confirm) and the Oct 30 Cup night
moments.timing: Late October (home opener date not verified)
moments.why: The first gameday merch wave of the season. The Cup opening game against the Nets on Oct 30 is an early home night.

moments.name: Black Friday and Cyber Week
moments.why: The first major discount window. It also lines up with Emirates NBA Cup group play.

moments.name: Boxing Day
moments.why: Canada's biggest in-store sale day and a gifting follow-up to the holidays. Whether the Raptors play at home that day is not yet confirmed.

moments.name: Lunar New Year
moments.why: Gifting and red-envelope season for Toronto's large Chinese and East Asian communities, and a chance for a Raptors heritage night.

moments.name: Playoffs and Jurassic Park viewing
moments.why: Watch-party crowds at Maple Leaf Square drive playoff tees, shorts and caps if the team advances.

moments.name: Caribana (Toronto Caribbean Carnival)
moments.timing: Early August, around the Civic Holiday
moments.why: The summer peak for Caribbean community fashion and street culture, and a moment for Black-community partnership.

moments.name: Back to school
moments.why: Youth sneaker and apparel buying ahead of Labour Day and school start.

moments.name: Diwali
moments.why: Gifting and new-clothes season for South Asian families across Brampton, Mississauga and Scarborough.

vocabulary.meaning: Local nickname for Toronto, popularised by Drake and used by fans on product and social.
The Raptors rallying slogan. Use only a few words, and mind the team and league licensing.
The day-after-Christmas sale and holiday in Canada. It has nothing to do with the sport.
The outdoor watch-party zone outside the arena at Maple Leaf Square.
Canadian two-dollar and one-dollar coins, used playfully in price talk.
Harmonized Sales Tax, 13% in Ontario, added at checkout.

designCues.cue: Raptors red and black with silver, plus a deep purple accent for retro lines
designCues.use: Make red the core fan-apparel anchor and rotate the secondary colours for seasonal drops.

designCues.cue: Cold-weather utility: water-resistant shell and fleece layers in charcoal
designCues.use: Specify water-resistant nylon shells, brushed fleece and toque-friendly cuts for the winter fan range.

designCues.cue: Canada maple leaf and national flag red used lightly, with care for licensing
designCues.source: Canadian identity for a national team
designCues.use: Use it as a subtle trim or label detail on a "Canada's team" tee, and check the rules on the Canadian flag and national symbols.

designCues.cue: Skyline and CN Tower line art as a Toronto graphic
designCues.use: Keep it to simple one-colour graphics on tees and hoodies. Don't copy third-party artwork.

designCues.cue: Kawhi-era 2019 championship nostalgia: black, gold and white trophy accents
designCues.use: Make a limited homecoming capsule that nods to 2019 without reusing league championship marks that require licensing.

designCues.cue: Multicultural pattern language drawn from partners, not borrowed
designCues.source: Toronto's Caribbean, South Asian, East African and Filipino communities
designCues.use: Commission artists from those communities for heritage-night patterns, and credit and pay them.

productHooks: Homecoming capsule: Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes tees, hoodies and kids' jerseys, launched before the home opener and held at full price until Black Friday.
Winter fan range: water-resistant warm-up jacket, fleece and toque in Raptors red, black and charcoal, made for the TTC and downtown walk to games.
Canada-only Boxing Day sale tier of non-hero Raptors product, kept apart from the City Edition and hero jerseys.
Heritage-night capsules (Caribana, Diwali, Lunar New Year), co-created with local artists and designers who are credited.
Kids' and youth swingman line with clear zero-rated pricing and school-season marketing in late August.
watchouts: We The North, Raptors marks and the Canadian flag and national symbols carry licensing and usage rules. Clear them before shipping.
Heritage and festival imagery (Caribana, Diwali, Lunar New Year) must come from community partners who are credited and paid. Avoid sacred or ceremonial iconography.
A story built mainly on Kawhi Leonard is exposed to his health and a short contract window. Keep team and city graphics central.
CAD pricing has to feel fair against US prices and discounts. Otherwise fans will cross the border or buy resale and knockoffs.
Don't present Drake or OVO as a partnership without confirmation. Treat any link as a conversation, not a plan.

channels.role: Eaton Centre, Yorkdale, Square One and chains such as Sport Chek and Foot Locker carry most in-person team and sneaker sales.
Fans across the country make online the default for jerseys. Free-shipping thresholds matter.
Toronto has a strong sneaker culture and reseller scene, so launches through the app and boutiques face heavy competition.
StockX, GOAT, Kijiji, Facebook Marketplace and Instagram sellers trade both sneakers and hard-to-get jerseys.
Scotiabank Arena merch, Maple Leaf Square and fan-fest events convert on emotion and gameday crowds.
Instagram and TikTok drive discovery. Community markets and independent vendor stalls feed lower-priced, sometimes unlicensed demand.

extra.priceProfile: Incomes range widely, from affluent North York and Yorkville shoppers to price-sensitive families in Scarborough, Brampton and the inner suburbs. Canadian prices already sit above US ones, with 13% HST on top. Tier clearly: a visible entry price for kids and tees, a core hoodie and jersey range, and a premium authentic and collaboration layer for drop-day buyers.
extra.jerseyBehavior: Fans buy swingman and replica jerseys of current stars (Barnes, Leonard), and fewer buy authentic ones. Kids' sizes and tees are the volume entry point. Some buy retro or Vince Carter-era jerseys as style pieces. Unlicensed knockoffs turn up in value-oriented markets, and many fans check sale windows and resale before paying full CAD price.
